easy.explanation: The speaker says, "In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust."
easy.q: In whom does the speaker place his trust?

easy.explanation: He asks God to deliver him, help him escape, and save him.
easy.q: What does the speaker ask God to do?

easy.explanation: Verse 5 says, "thou art my trust from my youth."
easy.q: Since when has the LORD been the speaker's trust?

medium.explanation: These images describe a safe place where the speaker can continually find refuge.
medium.q: What do "strong habitation," "rock," and "fortress" all communicate?

medium.explanation: To resort to a place is to go to it repeatedly, especially for protection.
medium.q: What does "continually resort" mean in verse 3?

answers: His life displays remarkable trust in God
medium.explanation: His continued dependence on God makes him an example or wonder to many people.
medium.q: Why is the speaker "as a wonder unto many"?

answers: Trust, deliverance, lifelong dependence, and witness to others
Old age, abandonment, silence, and defeat
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from trusting God for refuge to describing lifelong reliance and public testimony.

answers: The speaker's trust results in continual praise
The speaker no longer needs God
challenge.explanation: Because God has sustained him from birth, the speaker says his praise will continually be directed to God.
challenge.q: What does the phrase "my praise shall be continually of thee" reveal?

answers: God has been the speaker's hope and support throughout life
The speaker trusts only in future events
The speaker depends on human strength
challenge.explanation: Verse 5 calls God his hope and trust, while verse 6 says God upheld him from the womb.
challenge.q: What common idea appears in verses 5 and 6?

paragraphs.title: A Plea Not to Be Abandoned in Old Age

easy.explanation: He asks that his mouth be filled with God's praise and honour all the day.
easy.q: With what does the speaker want his mouth to be filled?

answers: In the time of old age
easy.explanation: He says, "Cast me not off in the time of old age."
easy.q: When does the speaker ask God not to cast him off?

easy.explanation: The enemies say, "God hath forsaken him."
easy.q: What do the speaker's enemies say about him?

answers: His enemies claim that God has abandoned him
He wants to stop praising God
He wants to teach his enemies music
medium.explanation: The enemies' threats lead him to ask God not to be far from him and to help quickly.
medium.q: Why does the speaker ask God to make haste for his help?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to a time of weakness and declining physical power.
medium.q: What does "when my strength faileth" mean?

answers: They should be confounded and covered with shame
medium.explanation: He asks that his adversaries be confounded, consumed, and covered with reproach and dishonour.
medium.q: What does the speaker ask to happen to those who seek his hurt?

answers: The speaker's praise of God versus the enemies' accusations
challenge.explanation: The speaker wants to praise God all day, while his enemies claim that God has forsaken him.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in verses 8–13?

answers: The speaker needs God's presence during weakness and danger
The speaker wants to avoid everyone
challenge.explanation: The requests not to be forsaken or left far away show his urgent need for divine help.
challenge.q: What is emphasized by the repeated requests for God to draw near and help?

answers: Both express the speaker's continuing need for God's protection
challenge.explanation: The speaker depends on God both when threatened by enemies and when weakened by age.
challenge.q: How are the requests for protection from enemies and from abandonment in old age related?

easy.explanation: He says, "But I will hope continually." The surrounding verses show that his hope is in God.
easy.q: In whom will the speaker continue to hope?

easy.explanation: He says, "I will yet praise thee more and more."
easy.q: What does the speaker promise to do more and more?

easy.explanation: The speaker says, "O God, thou hast taught me from my youth," and refers to God's wondrous works.
easy.q: What has God taught the speaker since his youth?

answers: The present generation and everyone who is to come
medium.explanation: He wants to show God's strength to "this generation" and His power to everyone who is to come.
medium.q: To whom does the speaker want to show God's strength and power?

medium.explanation: Wondrous works are remarkable acts that inspire wonder and praise.

answers: The speaker's lifelong experience motivates him to pass on God's greatness
It causes him to remain silent
It prevents him from praising God
medium.explanation: Having known God's works from youth, he wants to declare God's power to those who come after him.
medium.q: How does being taught from youth relate to speaking to future generations?

answers: The speaker attributes righteousness to God alone
challenge.explanation: The speaker will make mention of God's righteousness, specifically of God's righteousness alone.
challenge.q: What is emphasized by the phrase "even of thine only"?

answers: Personal hope and praise become a testimony for future generations
Praise changes into rejection of God
challenge.explanation: The speaker hopes, praises, remembers God's teaching, and then declares his works to coming generations.
challenge.q: What development takes place in verses 14–19?

answers: They are exceedingly great, and none is like God
They depend on the speaker's enemies
challenge.explanation: He declares that God's righteousness is very high and asks, "O God, who is like unto thee!"
challenge.q: What conclusion does the speaker reach about God's righteousness and greatness?

answers: Quicken him and bring him up again
easy.explanation: He trusts that God will quicken him again and bring him up from the depths of the earth.
easy.q: What does the speaker believe God will do after his troubles?

easy.explanation: He says, "I will also praise thee with the psaltery" and sing with the harp.
easy.q: Which instruments does the speaker mention for praising God?

easy.explanation: He says, "My tongue also shall talk of thy righteousness all the day long."
easy.q: What will the speaker's tongue talk about all day long?

answers: Increase his greatness and comfort him
medium.explanation: Verse 21 says, "Thou shalt increase my greatness, and comfort me on every side."
medium.q: What does the speaker ask God to do after bringing him up from the depths?

answers: Deep places of trouble and distress
medium.explanation: The phrase pictures a very low and difficult condition from which God can raise the speaker.
medium.q: What are "the depths of the earth" in this passage?

medium.explanation: God's promised rescue and comfort produce the speaker's thankful response.
medium.q: What leads the speaker to promise praise and singing?

answers: Being raised from the depths leads to thankful praise
challenge.explanation: The movement from the depths to praise shows deliverance leading to thanksgiving.
challenge.q: What connection exists between the depths of the earth and the singing at the end?

answers: It reinforces the speaker's confidence and his continued testimony about God's righteousness
It makes the speaker stop praising
It proves that God has abandoned him
challenge.explanation: After describing the shame of those seeking his hurt, the speaker continues to speak of God's righteousness.
challenge.q: What is the effect of the enemies being confounded and brought to shame?

answers: Trouble and depths, revival and comfort, then musical thanksgiving
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from distress to God's restoration and finally to praise with the psaltery and harp.
challenge.q: Which sequence best describes the passage's movement?
